{{Short description|Number that is the sum of its own digits, each raised to a given power}}
In [[number theory]], a '''perfect digital invariant (PDI)''' is a number in a given [[number base]] (<math>b</math>) that is the sum of its own digits each raised to a given [[Exponentiation|power]] (<math>p</math>).<ref name="moore2">[http://www.cs.umd.edu/Honors/reports/NarcissisticNums/NarcissisticNums.html ''Perfect and PluPerfect Digital Invariants''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071010035540/http://www.cs.umd.edu/Honors/reports/NarcissisticNums/NarcissisticNums.html |date=2007-10-10 }} by Scott Moore</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20091027123639/http://www.geocities.com/~harveyh/narciss.htm  PDIs] by Harvey Heinz</ref>

==Definition==
Let <math>n</math> be a [[natural number]]. The '''perfect digital invariant function''' (also known as a '''happy function''', from [[happy number]]s) for base <math>b > 1</math> and power <math>p > 0</math> <math>F_{p, b} : \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}</math> is defined as:
:<math>F_{p, b}(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{k - 1} d_i^p. </math>
where <math>k = \lfloor \log_{b}{n} \rfloor + 1</math> is the number of digits in the number in base <math>b</math>, and 
:<math>d_i = \frac{n \bmod{b^{i+1}} - n \bmod b^i}{b^i}</math>
is the value of each digit of the number. A natural number <math>n</math> is a '''perfect digital invariant''' if it is a [[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] for <math>F_{p, b}</math>, which occurs if <math>F_{p, b}(n) = n</math>. <math>0</math> and <math>1</math> are '''trivial perfect digital invariants''' for all <math>b</math> and <math>p</math>, all other perfect digital invariants are '''nontrivial perfect digital invariants'''.

For example, the number 4150 in base <math>b = 10</math> is a perfect digital invariant with <math>p = 5</math>, because <math>4150 = 4^5 + 1^5 + 5^5 + 0^5</math>.

A natural number <math>n</math> is a '''sociable digital invariant''' if it is a [[periodic point]] for <math>F_{p, b}</math>, where <math>F_{p,b}^k(n) = n</math> for a positive [[integer]] <math>k</math> (here <math>F_{p,b}^k</math> is the <math>k</math>th [[Iterated function|iterate]] of <math>F_{p,b}</math>), and forms a [[Periodic sequence|cycle]] of period <math>k</math>. A perfect digital invariant is a sociable digital invariant with <math>k = 1</math>, and a '''amicable digital invariant''' is a sociable digital invariant with <math>k = 2</math>.

All natural numbers <math>n</math> are [[periodic point#iterated function|preperiodic points]] for <math>F_{p, b}</math>, regardless of the base. This is because if <math>k \geq p + 2</math>, <math>n \geq b^{k-1} > b^p k</math>, so any <math>n</math> will satisfy <math>n > F_{b,p}(n)</math> until <math>n < b^{p+1}</math>. There are a finite number of natural numbers less than <math>b^{p+1}</math>, so the number is guaranteed to reach a periodic point or a fixed point less than <math> b^{p+1}</math>, making it a preperiodic point.

Numbers in base <math>b > p</math> lead to fixed or periodic points of numbers <math>n \leq (p - 2)^p + p (b - 1)^p</math>.

{{Math proof|title='''Proof'''|drop=hidden|proof=
If <math>b > p</math>, then the <math>n < b^{p+1}</math> bound can be reduced.
Let <math>r</math> be the number for which the sum of squares of digits is largest among the numbers less than <math>b^p</math>. 
:<math>r = b^p - 1 = \sum_{t=0}^p (b - 1)b^t</math>
:<math>F_{p, b}(r) = (p + 1)(b - 1)^p < (p + 1) b^p \leq b^{p + 1}</math> because <math>b \geq (p + 1)</math>
Let <math>s</math> be the number for which the sum of squares of digits is largest among the numbers less than <math>(p + 1)(b - 1)^p</math>.
:<math>s = (p + 1)b^p - 1 = p b^p + \sum_{t=0}^{p - 1} (b - 1)b^t</math>
:<math>F_{p, b}(s) = p^p + p (b - 1)^p < p b^p</math> because <math>b \geq p</math>
Let <math>t</math> be the number for which the sum of squares of digits is largest among the numbers less than <math>p b^p</math>.
:<math>t = (p - 1) b^p + \sum_{t=0}^{p - 1} (b - 1)b^t</math>
:<math>F_{p, b}(t) = (p - 1)^p + p (b - 1)^p</math>
Let <math>u</math> be the number for which the sum of squares of digits is largest among the numbers less than <math>F_{p, b}(t) + 1</math>.
:<math>u = (p - 2) b^p + \sum_{t=0}^{p - 1} (b - 1)b^t</math>
:<math>F_{p, b}(u) = (p - 2)^p + p (b - 1)^p < (p - 1)^p + p (b - 1)^p = n_{\ell+1}</math>
<math>u \leq F_{p, b}(u) < F_{p, b}(t)</math>. Thus, numbers in base <math>b > p</math> lead to cycles or fixed points of numbers <math>n \leq F_{p, b}(u) = (p - 1)^p + p (b - 1)^p</math>.
}}

The number of iterations <math>i</math> needed for <math>F_{p,b}^{i}(n)</math> to reach a fixed point is the perfect digital invariant function's [[persistence of a number|persistence]] of <math>n</math>, and undefined if it never reaches a fixed point.

<math>F_{1, b}</math> is the [[digit sum]]. The only perfect digital invariants are the single-digit numbers in base <math>b</math>, and there are no periodic points with prime period greater than 1.

<math>F_{p, 2}</math> reduces to <math>F_{1, 2}</math>, as for any power <math>p</math>, <math>0^p = 0</math> and <math>1^p = 1</math>.

For every natural number <math>k > 1</math>, if <math>p < b</math>, <math>(b - 1) \equiv 0 \bmod k</math> and <math>(p - 1) \equiv 0 \bmod \phi(k)</math>, then for every natural number <math>n</math>, if <math>n \equiv m \bmod k</math>, then <math>F_{p, b}(n) \equiv m \bmod k</math>, where <math>\phi(k)</math> is [[Euler's totient function]].
{{Math proof|title=Proof|drop=hidden|proof=
Let 
:<math>n = \sum_{i = 0}^j d_i b^i</math>
be a natural number with <math>j</math> digits, where <math>0 \leq d_i < b</math>, and <math>(b - 1) \equiv 0 \bmod k</math>, where <math>k</math> is a natural number greater than 1.

According to the [[divisibility rule]]s of base <math>b</math>, if <math>b - 1 \equiv 0 \bmod k</math>, then if <math>n \equiv m \bmod k</math>, then the [[digit sum]] 
: <math>F_{1, b}(n) = \sum_{i = 0}^j d_i \equiv m \bmod k</math>

If a digit <math>d_i \equiv m \bmod k</math>, then <math>d_i^p \equiv m^p \bmod k</math>. According to [[Euler's theorem]], if  <math>(p - 1) \equiv 0 \bmod \phi(k)</math>, <math>m^p \bmod k = m \bmod k</math>. Thus, if the [[digit sum]] <math>F_{1, b}(n) \equiv m \bmod k</math>, then <math>F_{p, b}(n) \equiv m \bmod k</math>.

Therefore, for any natural number <math>k</math>, if <math>p < b</math>, <math>(b - 1) \equiv 0 \bmod k</math> and <math>(p - 1) \equiv 0 \bmod \phi(k)</math>, then for every natural number <math>n</math>, if <math>n \equiv m \bmod k</math>, then <math>F_{p, b}(n) \equiv m \bmod k</math>.
}}

No upper bound can be determined for the size of perfect digital invariants in a given base and arbitrary power, and it is not currently known whether or not the number of perfect digital invariants for an arbitrary base is finite or infinite.<ref name="moore2"/>

==''F''<sub>2,''b''</sub>==
By definition, any three-digit perfect digital invariant <math>n = d_2 d_1 d_0</math> for <math>F_{2, b}</math> with natural number digits <math>0 \leq d_0 < b</math>, <math>0 \leq d_1 < b</math>, <math>0 \leq d_2 < b</math> has to satisfy the [[Cubic equation|cubic]] Diophantine equation <math>d_0^2 + d_1^2 + d_2^2 = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math>. <math>d_2</math> has to be equal to 0 or 1 for any <math>b > 2</math>, because the maximum value <math>n</math> can take is <math>n = (2 - 1)^2 + 2 (b - 1)^2 = 1 + 2 (b - 1)^2 < 2 b^2</math>. As a result, there are actually two related [[Quadratic equation|quadratic]] Diophantine equations to solve:
: <math>d_0^2 + d_1^2 = d_1 b + d_0</math> when <math>d_2 = 0</math>, and
: <math>d_0^2 + d_1^2 + 1 = b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math> when <math>d_2 = 1</math>.
The two-digit natural number <math>n = d_1 d_0</math> is a perfect digital invariant in base 
: <math>b = d_1 + \frac{d_0 (d_0 - 1)}{d_1}.</math>
This can be proven by taking the first case, where <math>d_2 = 0</math>, and solving for <math>b</math>. This means that for some values of <math>d_0</math> and <math>d_1</math>, <math>n</math> is not a perfect digital invariant in any base, as <math>d_1</math> is not a [[divisor]] of <math>d_0 (d_0 - 1)</math>. Moreover, <math>d_0 > 1</math>, because if <math>d_0 = 0</math> or <math>d_0 = 1</math>, then <math>b = d_1</math>, which contradicts the earlier statement that <math>0 \leq d_1 < b</math>.

There are no three-digit perfect digital invariants for <math>F_{2, b}</math>, which can be proven by taking the second case, where <math>d_2 = 1</math>, and letting <math>d_0 = b - a_0</math> and <math>d_1 = b - a_1</math>. Then the Diophantine equation for the three-digit perfect digital invariant becomes 
: <math>(b - a_0)^2 + (b - a_1)^2 + 1 = b^2 + (b - a_1) b + (b - a_0)</math>
: <math>b^2 - 2 a_0 b + a_0^2 + b^2 - 2 a_1 b + a_1^2 + 1 = b^2 + (b - a_1) b + (b - a_0)</math>
: <math>2 b^2 - 2 (a_0 + a_1) b + a_0^2 + a_1^2 + 1 = b^2 + (b - a_1) b + (b - a_0)</math>
: <math>b^2 + (b - 2 (a_0 + a_1)) b + a_0^2 + a_1^2 + 1 = b^2 + (b - a_1) b + (b - a_0)</math>
<math>2 (a_0 + a_1) > a_1</math> for all values of <math>0 < a_1 \leq b</math>. Thus, there are no solutions to the Diophantine equation, and there are no three-digit perfect digital invariants for <math>F_{2, b}</math>.

==''F''<sub>3,''b''</sub>==
{{Quote frame|
''There are just four numbers, after unity, which are the sums of the cubes of their digits:''

:<math>153=1^3+5^3+3^3</math>
:<math>370=3^3+7^3+0^3</math>
:<math> 371=3^3+7^3+1^3</math>
:<math>407=4^3+0^3+7^3.</math>
''These are odd facts, very suitable for puzzle columns and likely to amuse amateurs, but there is nothing in them which appeals to the mathematician.'' {{OEIS|id=A046197}}|[[G. H. Hardy]]|[[A Mathematician's Apology]]}}

By definition, any four-digit perfect digital invariant <math>n</math> for <math>F_{3, b}</math> with natural number digits <math>0 \leq d_0 < b</math>, <math>0 \leq d_1 < b</math>, <math>0 \leq d_2 < b</math>, <math>0 \leq d_3 < b</math> has to satisfy the [[Quartic equation|quartic]] Diophantine equation <math>d_0^3 + d_1^3 + d_2^3 + d_3^3 = d_3 b^3 + d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math>. <math>d_3</math> has to be equal to 0, 1, 2 for any <math>b > 3</math>, because the maximum value <math>n</math> can take is <math>n = (3 - 2)^3 + 3 (b - 1)^3 = 1 + 3 (b - 1)^3 < 3 b^3</math>. As a result, there are actually three related [[Cubic equation|cubic]] Diophantine equations to solve
: <math>d_0^3 + d_1^3 + d_2^3 = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math> when <math>d_3 = 0</math>
: <math>d_0^3 + d_1^3 + d_2^3 + 1 = b^3 + d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math> when <math>d_3 = 1</math>
: <math>d_0^3 + d_1^3 + d_2^3 + 8 = 2 b^3 + d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math> when <math>d_3 = 2</math>
We take the first case, where <math>d_3 = 0</math>.

=== ''b'' = 3''k'' + 1 ===
Let <math>k</math> be a positive integer and the number base <math>b = 3 k + 1</math>. Then:
*<math>n_1 = kb^2 + (2k + 1)b</math> is a perfect digital invariant for <math>F_{3, b}</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
{{Math proof|title=Proof|drop=hidden|proof=
Let the digits of <math>n_1 = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math> be <math>d_2 = k</math>, <math>d_1 = 2k + 1</math>, and <math>d_0 = 0</math>. Then
: <math>
\begin{align}
F_{3, b}(n_1) & = d_0^3 + d_1^3 + d_2^3 \\
& = k^3 + (2k + 1)^3 + 0^3 \\
& = (k^2 - k(2k + 1) + (2k + 1)^2)(k + (2k + 1)) \\
& = (k^2 - 2k^2 - k + 4k^2 + 4k + 1)(3k + 1) \\
& = (3k^2 + 3k + 1)(3k + 1) \\
& = (3k^2 + 4k + 1)(3k + 1) - k(3k + 1) \\
& = (k + 1)(3k + 1)(3k + 1) - k(3k + 1) \\
& = k(3k + 1)(3k + 1) + (3k + 1)(3k + 1) - k(3k + 1) \\
& = k(3k + 1)^2 + (2k + 1)(3k + 1) + 0 \\
& = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0 \\
& = n_1
\end{align}
</math>
Thus <math>n_1</math> is a perfect digital invariant for <math>F_{3, b}</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
}}
*<math>n_2 = kb^2 + (2k + 1)b + 1</math> is a perfect digital invariant for <math>F_{3, b}</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
{{Math proof|title=Proof|drop=hidden|proof=
Let the digits of <math>n_2 = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math> be <math>d_2 = k</math>, <math>d_1 = 2k + 1</math>, and <math>d_0 = 1</math>. Then
:<math>
\begin{align}
F_{3, b}(n_2) & = d_0^3 + d_1^3 + d_2^3 \\
& = k^3 + (2k + 1)^3 + 1^3 \\
& = (k^2 - k(2k + 1) + (2k + 1)^2)(k + (2k + 1)) + 1 \\
& = (k^2 - 2k^2 - k + 4k^2 + 4k + 1)(3k + 1) + 1 \\
& = (3k^2 + 3k + 1)(3k + 1) + 1 \\
& = (3k^2 + 4k + 1)(3k + 1) - k(3k + 1) + 1 \\
& = (k + 1)(3k + 1)(3k + 1) - k(3k + 1) + 1 \\
& = k(3k + 1)(3k + 1) + (3k + 1)(3k + 1) - k(3k + 1) + 1 \\
& = k(3k + 1)^2 + (2k + 1)(3k + 1) + 1 \\
& = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0 \\
& = n_2
\end{align}
</math>
Thus <math>n_2</math> is a perfect digital invariant for <math>F_{3, b}</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
}}
*<math>n_3 = (k + 1)b^2 + (2k + 1)</math> is a perfect digital invariant for <math>F_{3, b}</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
{{Math proof|title=Proof|drop=hidden|proof=
Let the digits of <math>n_3 = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math> be <math>d_2 = k + 1</math>, <math>d_1 = 0</math>, and <math>d_0 = 2k + 1</math>. Then
:<math>
\begin{align}
F_{3, b}(n_3) & = d_0^3 + d_1^3 + d_2^3 \\
& = (k + 1)^3 + 0^3 + (2k + 1)^3 \\
& = ((k + 1)^2 - (k + 1)(2k + 1) + (2k + 1)^2)((k + 1) + (2k + 1)) \\
& = ((k + 1)^2 + k(2k + 1)(3k + 2) \\
& = (k^2 + 2k + 1 + 2k^2 + k)(3k + 2) \\
& = (3k^2 + 3k + 1)(3k + 2) \\
& = (3k^2 + 3k)(3k + 2) + (3k + 2) \\
& = 3k(k + 1)(3k + 2) + (3k + 2) \\
& = (k + 1)((3k + 1)^2 - 1) + (3k + 2) \\
& = (k + 1)(3k + 1)^2 - (k + 1) + (3k + 2) \\
& = (k + 1)(3k + 1)^2 + 0(3k + 1) + (2k + 1) \\
& = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0 \\
& = n_3
\end{align}
</math>
Thus <math>n_3</math> is a perfect digital invariant for <math>F_{3, b}</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
}}

=== ''b'' = 3''k'' + 2 ===
Let <math>k</math> be a positive integer and the number base <math>b = 3 k + 2</math>. Then:
*<math>n_1 = kb^2 + (2k + 1)</math> is a perfect digital invariant for <math>F_{3, b}</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
{{Math proof|title=Proof|drop=hidden|proof=
Let the digits of <math>n_1 = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math> be <math>d_2 = k</math>, <math>d_1 = 2k + 1</math>, and <math>d_0 = 0</math>. Then
: <math>F_{3, b}(n_1) = d_0^3 + d_1^3 + d_2^3</math>
:: <math> = k^3 + 0^3 + (2k + 1)^3</math>
:: <math> = (k^2 - k(2k + 1) + (2k + 1)^2)(k + (2k + 1))</math>
:: <math> = (k^2 - 2k^2 - k + 4k^2 + 4k + 1)(3k + 1)</math>
:: <math> = (3k^2 + 3k + 1)(3k + 1)</math>
:: <math> = (3k^2 + 3k + 1)(3k + 2) - (3k^2 + 3k + 1)</math>
:: <math> = (3k^2 + 3k + 1)(3k + 2) - (3k^2 + 2k + k + 1)</math>
:: <math> = (3k^2 + 3k + 1)(3k + 2) - k(3k + 2) - (k + 1)</math>
:: <math> = (3k^2 + 2k + 1)(3k + 2) - (k + 1)</math>
:: <math> = (3k^2 + 2k)(3k + 2) + (3k + 2) - (k + 1)</math>
:: <math> = k(3k + 2)^2 + (2k + 1)</math>
:: <math> = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math>
:: <math> = n_1</math>
Thus <math>n_1</math> is a perfect digital invariant for <math>F_{3, b}</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
}}

=== ''b'' = 6''k'' + 4 ===
Let <math>k</math> be a positive integer and the number base <math>b = 6 k + 4</math>. Then:
*<math>n_4 = kb^2 + (3k + 2)b + (2k + 1)</math> is a perfect digital invariant for <math>F_{3, b}</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
{{Math proof|title=Proof|drop=hidden|proof=
Let the digits of <math>n_4 = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math> be <math>d_2 = k + 1</math>, <math>d_1 = 3k + 2</math>, and <math>d_0 = 2k + 1</math>. Then
:<math>F_{3, b}(n_3) = d_0^3 + d_1^3 + d_2^3</math>
::<math> = (k)^3 + (3k + 2)^3 + (2k + 1)^3</math>
::<math> = k^3 + ((3k + 2)^2 - (3k + 2)(2k + 1) + (2k + 1)^2)((3k + 2) + (2k + 1))</math>
::<math> = k^3 + ((3k + 2)(k + 1) + (2k + 1)^2)(5k + 3)</math>
::<math> = k^3 + (3k^2 + 5k + 2 + 4k^2 + 4k + 1)(5k + 3)</math>
::<math> = k^3 + (7k^2 + 9k + 3)(5k + 3)</math>
::<math> = k^3 + 5k(7k^2 + 9k + 3) + 3(7k^2 + 9k + 3)</math>
::<math> = k^3 + 35k^3 + 45k^2 + 15k + 21k^2 + 27k + 9</math>
::<math> = 36k^3 + 66k^2 + 42k + 9</math>
::<math> = (6k + 4)(6k^2) + 42k^2 + 42k + 9</math>
::<math> = (6k + 4)(6k^2) + (6k + 4)(4k^2) + 18k^2 + 26k + 9</math>
::<math> = (6k + 4)(6k^2 + 4k) + 18k^2 + 26k + 9</math>
::<math> = k(6k + 4)^2 + (6k + 4)(3k) + 14k + 9</math>
::<math> = k(6k + 4)^2 + (3k + 2)(6k + 4) + 2k + 1</math>
::<math> = d_2 b^2 + d_1 b + d_0</math>
:: <math> = n_4</math>
Thus <math>n_4</math> is a perfect digital invariant for <math>F_{3, b}</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
}}

==Extension to negative integers==
Perfect digital invariants can be extended to the negative integers by use of a [[signed-digit representation]] to represent each integer.

=== Balanced ternary ===
In [[balanced ternary]], the digits are 1, −1 and 0. This results in the following:
* With [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] powers <math>p \equiv 1 \bmod 2</math>, <math>F_{p, \text{bal}3}</math> reduces down to [[digit sum]] iteration, as <math>(-1)^p = -1</math>, <math>0^p = 0</math> and <math>1^p = 1</math>.
* With [[parity (mathematics)|even]] powers <math>p \equiv 0 \bmod 2</math>, <math>F_{p, \text{bal}3}</math> indicates whether the number is even or odd, as the sum of each digit will indicate divisibility by 2 [[if and only if]] the sum of digits ends in 0. As <math>0^p = 0</math> and <math>(-1)^p = 1^p = 1</math>, for every pair of digits 1 or −1, their sum is 0 and the sum of their squares is 2.

==Relation to happy numbers==
{{Main|Happy number}}
A happy number <math>n</math> for a given base <math>b</math> and a given power <math>p</math> is a preperiodic point for the perfect digital invariant function <math>F_{p, b}</math> such that the <math>m</math>-th iteration of <math>F_{p, b}</math> is equal to the trivial perfect digital invariant <math>1</math>, and an unhappy number is one such that there exists no such <math>m</math>.

==Programming example==
The example below implements the perfect digital invariant function described in the definition above [[Cycle detection|to search for perfect digital invariants and cycles]] in [[Python (programming language)|Python]]. This can be used to find [[happy numbers]].
<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
def pdif(x: int, p: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Perfect digital invariant function."""
    total = 0
    while x > 0:
        total = total + pow(x % b, p)
        x = x // b
    return total

def pdif_cycle(x: int, p: int, b: int) -> list[int]:
    seen = []
    while x not in seen:
        seen.append(x)
        x = pdif(x, p, b)
    cycle = []
    while x not in cycle:
        cycle.append(x)
        x = pdif(x, p, b)
    return cycle
</syntaxhighlight>
